matching.reasoningTemplate: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with weight loss suggests an IBD flare, but infective colitis must be excluded first.

clinicalPearls: UC inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally without skip areas, whereas Crohn's is segmental with skip lesions and frequently spares the rectum; this distribution difference is a key way to separate the two (p.2555-2556).

Granulomas (noncaseating, in all bowel-wall layers) are characteristic of Crohn's but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens, so their absence does not exclude Crohn's (p.2556).
On biopsy, distorted/branching crypt architecture and basal plasmacytosis/lymphoid aggregates indicate chronicity and help distinguish IBD from acute self-limited or infectious colitis (p.2556).

Faecal calprotectin and lactoferrin correlate with histologic inflammation, help predict relapse, and can detect pouchitis; they are used to distinguish active inflammation from IBS or bacterial overgrowth (p.2556-2557).
Distinguishing UC from Crohn's is not possible initially in up to ~15% of cases (indeterminate colitis), though the true type usually declares itself later (p.2559).
Only ~15% of UC patients present initially with severe disease (p.2557).
Distal/proctitis-limited UC can paradoxically present with constipation due to slowed proximal transit despite distal inflammation (p.2557).
In severely ill UC patients serum albumin falls quickly; leukocytosis can occur but is not a specific marker of disease activity (p.2557).
harrison.pathophysiology: IBD is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract regarded as a dysregulated, inappropriate immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host. Homeostasis among the gut microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells, and mucosal immune system is normally maintained by regulatory pathways (e.g., FoxP3 T-regulatory cells); environmental factors (smoking, antibiotics, enteropathogens, diet) acting on genetic susceptibility (>240 GWAS loci, ~20% of risk explained; rare single-gene defects such as IL10/IL10R in very-early-onset disease) disrupt this balance and produce sustained inflammation. UC is a mucosal/superficial-submucosal disease, while Crohn's is transmural with fissuring and fistula/stricture formation (p.2551-2556).
additionalDifferentials: Indeterminate colitis (UC vs Crohn's cannot be distinguished early in up to 15% of cases) (p.2559)
Diverticulitis / diverticular-associated colitis (mimics Crohn's clinically and radiographically) (p.2560)

Ischaemic colitis (consider in the elderly, hypercoagulable states, post-AAA repair; abrupt left lower quadrant pain with red rectal bleeding and a normal rectum with a sharp transition) (p.2560-2561)
Collagenous and lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis - normal endoscopic appearance, chronic watery diarrhoea (p.2561)
NSAID-related colitis (de novo, or reactivation of IBD) (p.2561)
Behcet's syndrome, graft-versus-host disease, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, neutropenic colitis (p.2560)
infectionMimics: Clostridioides difficile colitis (watery diarrhoea, tenesmus, nausea, vomiting) (p.2560)
Campylobacter colitis (can mimic severe UC endoscopically and can trigger a relapse of established UC) (p.2559)
Shigella (watery diarrhoea then tenesmus and bloody mucoid stool) (p.2559)
Yersinia enterocolitica (terminal ileum involvement mimicking Crohn's ileitis) (p.2559-2560)
Enterohaemorrhagic / enteroinvasive / enteroadherent E. coli (bloody diarrhoea) (p.2560)

Cytomegalovirus colitis (abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, fever, weight loss; can occur in immunocompetent hosts; severe disease can cause necrosis and perforation; diagnosed by intranuclear inclusions on biopsy) (p.2560)
Herpes simplex proctitis (anorectal/perianal; can occur in immunocompetent individuals) (p.2560)
Gastrointestinal tuberculosis / Mycobacterium avium (distal ileal and cecal disease mimicking Crohn's) (p.2560)
Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic colitis; fulminant form mortality >50%) (p.2560-2561)
Other parasites: Isospora belli, hookworm, Trichuris trichiura, Strongyloides (p.2561)
additionalInvestigations: Acute-phase reactants - CRP, platelet count and ESR rise; haemoglobin falls in active disease (p.2556-2557)
Serum albumin (falls quickly in severe illness) (p.2557)
Faecal lactoferrin (sensitive/specific marker of intestinal inflammation) (p.2556)

Sigmoidoscopy to assess activity before treatment; full colonoscopy (deferred during an acute flare) to assess extent and activity, with multiple biopsies including from normal-appearing mucosa (p.2556-2557)
Intestinal ultrasound to assess activity and mucosal healing (p.2557)
Surveillance colonoscopy with biopsies (chromoendoscopy in higher-risk patients) for dysplasia/cancer in long-standing colitis (p.2570)
redFlags: Toxic megacolon - transverse or right colon dilated >6 cm with loss of haustration during a severe attack; surgical emergency, can be precipitated by electrolyte abnormalities and narcotics (p.2557)
Perforation - the most dangerous local complication; signs of peritonitis may be masked by glucocorticoids; mortality of perforation complicating toxic megacolon is ~15% (p.2557)
Toxic colitis with deep ulceration - bowel may perforate without first dilating (p.2557)
Massive haemorrhage (occurs in ~1% of UC patients) (p.2557)
High-spiking fever in Crohn's suggesting intraabdominal abscess (p.2557)
Colonic stricture that prevents colonoscope passage - presume malignant until proven otherwise (indication for surgery) (p.2557)
harrison.prognosis: Toxic megacolon occurs rarely; about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, but those that do not require urgent colectomy. Perforation complicating toxic megacolon carries ~15% mortality. Risk of colorectal cancer rises with duration and extent of colitis (historically ~2% at 10 yr, 8% at 20 yr, 18% at 30 yr, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; still ~1.5-2x the general population). Extensive long-standing colitis carries the highest cancer risk. Strictures occur in ~5% of UC patients. Up to one-third of IBD patients develop at least one extraintestinal manifestation (p.2557-2563, p.2570).
pitfalls: Before escalating immunosuppression in a presumed flare, exclude superimposed infection - C. difficile and CMV colitis can mimic or complicate IBD; diagnosis requires negative stool studies (culture, C. difficile toxin, ova and parasites) and, for CMV, identification of intranuclear inclusions on mucosal biopsy (p.2557, p.2560).

A first 'flare' of bloody diarrhoea may actually be an infectious colitis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile, amoebic) - infection should be excluded before diagnosing IBD; Campylobacter and others can also reactivate established UC (p.2559-2560).
Granulomas are frequently absent on mucosal biopsy even in Crohn's, so their absence does not rule it out (p.2556).
Effective medical therapy can normalise mucosal appearance and create apparent skip areas in UC, mimicking Crohn's distribution; biopsy normal-appearing mucosa (p.2555-2556).
Extensive perianal lesions in a patient labelled UC should raise suspicion for Crohn's instead (p.2557).
In patients on glucocorticoids, peritoneal signs of perforation may be blunted/absent (p.2557).
An impassable colonic stricture should be presumed malignant rather than benign inflammatory (p.2557).
harrison.severityClassification: Montreal classification of UC severity (Harrison Table 337-4, p.2557): S0 clinical remission (no symptoms); S1 mild = up to 4 stools/day +/- blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate = 4 or more stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe = 6 or more bloody stools/day plus pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5 C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, and ESR >=30 mm/h. (These severe-disease physiologic thresholds mirror the classic Truelove-Witts criteria for acute severe colitis.) Montreal extent: E1 proctitis, E2 left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), E3 extensive/pancolitis. Crohn's is categorised by the Vienna/Montreal classification (Table 337-5, p.2558) by age at diagnosis (A), location ileal/colonic/ileocolonic/upper (L), and behaviour nonstricturing-nonpenetrating/stricturing/penetrating (B) with a perianal modifier.
